Nvidia CEO Discloses Affair, Board Launches Probe Over Chinese Spy Fears
 
Plus, elections in the U.S. and Europe are getting more volatile, and 20-somethings are ditching entry-level jobs to become their own bosses
 
 
SEAN GALLUP/GETTY IMAGES
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

When the chief executive of a $4 trillion tech giant discloses an affair, Wall Street takes notice. When that relationship entangles him with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, it quickly raises questions of national security.

 

Nvidia’s board said it is launching an investigation into the matter, while expressing confidence in its co-founder.

 

The investigation comes as Huang lobbies the U.S. government and leaders around the world to allow the free flow of chips powering the latest AI models and attempts to rebut concerns that such an approach could compromise national security.

 

This morning, we examine the espionage inquiry encircling one of Silicon Valley’s most powerful executives, alongside a closer look at the family dynasty helping him run Nvidia.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• In his first sit-down interview since Republicans’ devastating election losses, President Trump floated a deal with Democrats on immigration, suggested he might not endorse a Republican successor ahead of the 2028 election and said he had no intention of forgiving his political enemies.

 

• The massive shift in the midterm elections is a sign of a new political era taking hold from the U.S. to Europe.

 

• China’s push for influence in the South Pacific is running into resistance.

• For big bank stocks, Capitol Hill’s bark is worse than its bite, writes Telis Demos.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Democrats promised to fix the economy. What can they really do?

 

The voters who powered the Democrats’ triumph in the midterms delivered a blunt message: Make the economy work for us. Now, Democrats must deliver. Whether they can isn’t assured, despite the party’s pending control of the House and Senate. Many demands are beyond the reach of lawmakers to fix. The main tools of Congress, taxes and spending, are limited and slow-moving—and lawmakers still face Trump’s veto. Satisfying voter wishes also could have unintended consequences, report Matt Grossman, Jeanne Whalen and Gavin Bade.

 

5.

 

Dwindling pay is fueling high-profile exits from Blackstone’s marquee real-estate team.

 

A string of high-level departures from Blackstone’s real-estate business is shaking up the world’s biggest property investor. Nearly a third of the unit’s senior managing directors have left the firm over the past three years as its investment funds for the sector have slumped. Each of the dozen Blackstone real-estate executives departed for a variety of reasons. Some became weary of a job that demanded constant travel and being on call nonstop. Others retired or were eased out. But a common thread runs through the mini-exodus: They were no longer making the money they had in their best years because Blackstone’s real-estate funds aren’t earning as much. And with borrowing costs high and commercial real estate struggling, industry executives don’t see prospects for that changing soon, reports Peter Grant.

6. SEE THE STORY

EMMA BROWN
 

Violent gangs vying to control cocaine exports have destabilized once-peaceful Ecuador. In northern Africa’s Sahel region, religious insurgents and ethnic militias have chased government authorities from entire provinces. And in Southeast Asia, criminal syndicates run industrial-scale fraud centers and drug operations from ungoverned pockets of Myanmar and Cambodia. Around the world, guerrillas, cartels and syndicates are challenging traditional concepts of nationhood as they use violence and coercion to exert dominance over territory and people. More than 200 million people across 60 countries live in areas controlled or contested by armed nonstate groups, according to International Committee of the Red Cross estimates.

8. THE NUMBER

 
23%
 

At least 23% of Americans between 18 and 34 were running their own business or side hustle last year, up from 19% in 2021, according to Babson College. Among those from ages 18 to 24, that rate has more than doubled from a decade ago. No demographic is launching enterprises faster than 20-somethings: As AI disrupts the entry-level jobs once seen as reliable career steppingstones, younger workers are deploying the technology to bypass corporate ladders and build companies of their own.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Meet the parents building bowling alleys and wellness spas to keep their kids home.

 

Wealthy homeowners across the country are spending millions on amenities designed to draw their teenage and adult children back home. The hope is that features like golf simulators, juice bars, vending machines and dance studios—often costing hundreds of thousands of dollars—will encourage more family time. Many are finding, however, that salons and pickleball courts only go so far.
